title: Global sections of a proper scheme
statement:
Let $k$ be a field and $X$ a proper scheme over $k$ [def-pc-morphism-conventions].

1. If $X$ is a variety over $k$ [def-pc-curve], then $H^0(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$ is a finite field extension of $k$.
2. If $X$ is geometrically integral over $k$ [def-pc-geometrically-irreducible], then $H^0(X,\mathcal{O}_X)=k$ as $k$-algebras.

proof.text: (1) Put $A=H^0(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$. The structure morphism $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}(k)$ is proper, so the finite-dimensionality clause of [lem-pc-euler-characteristic-well-defined] gives that $A$ is finite-dimensional over $k$. Since $X$ is a variety, it is integral by [def-pc-curve]. Let $\eta$ be its generic point. By [lem-sc-integral-scheme-stalks-in-function-field], the restriction $A=\mathcal O_X(X)\to\mathcal O_{X,\eta}=k(X)$ is injective, so $A$ is a domain. The Mathlib leaf [lem-weil-pbc-finite-dimensional-domain-is-field] applied to the finite-dimensional $k$-algebra $A$ shows that $A$ is a field. Thus $A$ is a finite field extension of $k$.

source.place: Tag 04L2 (lemma-regular-functions-proper-variety), clause (1), via Tag 0BUG (lemma-proper-geometrically-reduced-global-sections), clauses (1) and (3); proof here expands the field argument through the cited DAG nodes

proof.text: (2) Put $A=H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)$ and let $\bar k$ be an algebraic closure of $k$. Since $X$ is proper and $k\to\bar k$ is flat, [lem-sc-flat-base-change-coherent] identifies $H^0(X_{\bar k},\mathcal O_{X_{\bar k}})$ with $A\otimes_k\bar k$. Geometric integrality means that $X_{\bar k}$ is integral [def-pc-geometrically-irreducible], and it remains proper over $\bar k$ by [lem-pc-proper-base-change]; hence it is a variety over $\bar k$ [def-pc-curve]. Applying (1) over $\bar k$ shows that $A\otimes_k\bar k$ is a finite field extension of $\bar k$. By [lem-pc-finite-extension-alg-closed], $A\otimes_k\bar k=\bar k$. The scalar-extension dimension formula [lem-pc-finrank-field-base-change] gives $\dim_k A=\dim_{\bar k}(A\otimes_k\bar k)=1$. The unit map $k\to A$ is an injective $k$-linear map between one-dimensional vector spaces, hence an isomorphism of $k$-algebras; therefore $A=k$.
